summary: Rand describes how it uses remote job entry on the network. Users build a job deck in the Rand file system, send it to UCLA's remote job service with an access program, and monitor the job's status. A sample session is included.

eli5.summary: You write a job on your computer, send it to a bigger computer far away to run, and check its progress.

questions: how did early networks handle batch jobs
how did arpanet users submit jobs
subtitle: How Rand computers accessed UCLA's remote job service over the early network

tldr.problem: In 1972, only large computers like UCLA's mainframe could run big batch jobs, and getting access to one from afar was complex and manual.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 307 documents how Rand's PDP-10 computer ran a program called RJSAP (RJS Access Program) that let users submit jobs to UCLA's IBM 360/91 over the network, monitor their progress, and retrieve results.
tldr.outcome: Users at other network sites could now access UCLA's powerful computing resources by logging into Rand and running RJSAP, making large-scale computing accessible to more organizations.

today: RFC 307 is an early documentation of practical network use on ARPANET, now of historical interest. Remote job entry and batch processing have evolved into modern cloud computing, but the concept of submitting work to a remote system remains.

sections.title: Remote Job Entry in 1972
sections.content: In the early 1970s, most organizations did not have their own powerful computers. The solution was to use remote job entry (RJE): you prepared your job on a local machine, sent it to a remote facility with a powerful mainframe, and retrieved the results. Rand Corporation had been using RJE to send jobs to UCLA's IBM 360/91 for over a year by the time this RFC was written in February 1972. When Rand's PDP-10 joined the network, staff created RJSAP to automate this process.
sections.eli5: Long ago, if you needed a big computer to run a job, you would write out your work, mail it to a place with a big computer, wait for them to run it, and get the results back.

sections.title: How RJSAP Works
sections.content: A user at Rand would log into the PDP-10 and type RJS to start RJSAP. The program checked the user's credentials to confirm they had a valid RJS terminal ID at UCLA. It then opened a network connection to UCLA's RJS (Remote Job Service) and signed on the user. From there, the user could send a job deck (a file containing their batch job), check the job's status, and request printed output be returned. Commands were simple: S to send a job, PR to get printer output, / to send commands directly to UCLA's system, and Q to quit.
sections.eli5: You log in, run a program that connects to the far-away computer, upload your job, check its progress, and download the results.

sections.title: A Sample Session
sections.content: The RFC includes a full sample session. A user logs in to Rand, starts RJSAP, and is greeted. After confirming the RJS service is ready, they type S to send a job from file TESTA. Both RJSAP and UCLA's RJS acknowledge the submission. The user can then type /STATUS JOBS to see their job being queued, spooled, executed, and eventually show print output ready. Finally, they type PR to retrieve the printed output to a printer device, check transmission progress with R, and quit with Q.
sections.eli5: You pick your job file, send it, ask 'is it done yet?' a few times, get the results, and log off.
